claim: Both sides debate F1/recall/drift as if the inputs are trustworthy, but neither interrogates the measurement apparatus itself - the Time-ordered drift split, the Time feature inside the model, the single-seed single-threshold evaluation, and the absence of a business-cost objective all undermine the very numbers bull and bear are arguing over.
evidence: Neither side notices that `Time` is in metrics.json feature_columns AND is the exact variable used by drift-monitor to cut baseline vs new batch (drift_report.json baseline_rows=142404, new_batch_rows=142403 - a perfect 50/50 Time split of 284,807 rows) - so the model can learn a Time-dependent shortcut and the drift signal is partly tautological: we trained on Time and then measured drift along Time.

Bear cites 'max |rel_delta|=2.0000 on V3' and bull concedes it, but neither notices the rel_delta values for V1-V28 are all suspiciously close to +/-2.0000 - that is the algebraic signature of zero-mean PCA features being split into two halves with opposite signs (mean flips, denominator ~0, ratio saturates at 2). The 'drift' may be a metric artifact of computing rel_delta on features whose population mean is engineered to be ~0, not a genuine distribution shift.

Bull claims F1=0.8586 meets the >=0.85 bar and bear claims it is fragile - but neither asks whether F1 is even the right objective for fraud, where a missed fraud (FN) costs the face value of the transaction while a false positive (FP) costs only analyst review time. A 11-FP/16-FN split is not obviously better or worse than, say, 50-FP/5-FN without a cost matrix that neither bull nor bear supplies.

metrics.json shows attempts=1 with random_state=42 and a single train/test split - neither side demands a seed-variance check, k-fold, or bootstrap CI on F1. With only 98 positives in the test fold, a 95% CI on recall is roughly +/-7 percentage points; the 0.0086 margin over the 0.85 bar (bull) and the 16/98 recall gap (bear) may both be inside noise.

Both sides accept the default 0.5 decision threshold implicit in the confusion matrix, but AUC=0.9684 means the threshold is a free parameter - the operating point that produced 11 FP / 16 FN was never justified against a PR curve or a business cost function, so arguing about precision vs recall at that specific point is arguing about an arbitrary choice.

Bear says scale_pos_weight=577.29 is 'miscalibrated to current base rate' after the class-rate shift, and bull says weighting 'properly corrects' for imbalance - but neither asks whether the model's predicted probabilities are calibrated at all (no Brier score, no reliability diagram in metrics.json), which matters more than scale_pos_weight for any downstream threshold or cost-based decisioning.
challenges: What is the per-transaction cost matrix (FN dollar loss vs FP analyst-minutes) that would convert metrics.json into an expected-value comparison, and why is neither bull nor bear citing it?

If drift_report.json were recomputed with a random-shuffle baseline/new split instead of a Time-median split, would rel_delta collapse to ~0 - i.e., is 'drift_detected=true' actually a property of the data or of the splitting rule?

What is the seed-variance and bootstrap 95% CI of F1 across, say, 20 random_states on the same 80/20 stratified split - does the 0.8586 point estimate overlap the 0.85 bar once uncertainty is quantified?
